title: 2025 Legal Department Operations (LDO) Index
author: Thomson Reuters Institute · Buying Legal Council

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s emphasis on organisational complements and adds concrete buyer-side evidence that tool access alone is insufficient: underuse of existing legal technology indicates weak AI readiness, supporting stronger implementation, training and integration before adoption accelerates. It does not address verification or apprenticeship risks directly.
qs: As corporate legal departments rush to adopt AI, a new report shows that many existing legal tech tools are underutilized, which means that departments are not even taking full advantage of the technologies they’re already deployed  ## Key insights:*  *More focus on implementation, training, and integration is needed ***— Many legal departments need to be more prepared before accelerating their AI adoption plans.
There are vital lessons and warnings that legal departments should heed, however, as they rush to adopt AI and other emerging technologies.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central proposition that AI value depends on organisational absorption rather than tool acquisition alone. It materially extends that proposition with 2025 survey evidence of technology underutilisation in US corporate legal departments and concrete recommendations on workflow redesign, governance, implementation capacity, training and change management, while remaining cautious about readiness and realised efficiency.
qs: The underutilization of existing technology in legal departments isn't just a current operational challenge — it's a warning signal about departments’ readiness for the AI era.
In addition, AI adoption will require more substantial changes to departmental workflows, role definitions, and work practices than previous technology deployments.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central proposition that legal departments may capture AI gains only if they overcome organisational absorption constraints. It distinguishes rising investment and adoption ambitions from realised effectiveness, identifying workflow redesign, integration, training and change management—not procurement alone—as prerequisites for operational transformation.
qs: Corporate legal departments can't simply purchase AI tools and expect them to magically generate efficiency from day one.
In addition, AI adoption will require more substantial changes to departmental workflows, role definitions, and work practices than previous technology deployments.

st.t: Legal departments: AI supports selective sourcing redesign
st.an: The LDO Index supports the cluster’s account of buyer-side transformation under resource pressure while reinforcing its evidentiary cautions. It reports rising workloads, under-resourcing and constrained budgets alongside planned automation and insourcing, but distinguishes these intentions from achieved cost savings or mature technology deployment.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that AI adoption is accelerating but that durable value depends on implementation, training, integration and organisational readiness rather than technology acquisition alone. It also reinforces the distinction between expected efficiency gains and demonstrated returns, while offering little evidence on provider bargaining or pricing change.
qs: As corporate legal departments rush to adopt AI, a new report shows that many existing legal tech tools are underutilized, which means that departments are not even taking full advantage of the technologies they’re already deployed  ## Key insights:*  *More focus on implementation, training, and integration is needed ***— Many legal departments need to be more prepared before accelerating their AI adoption plans.
- ***Use of legal technology is expected to increase ***— Many legal departments report increasing or stable budgets for technology investments.

kp.k: Survey and spend analytics provide distinct evidence bases
kp.d: The report announcement describes a July survey of 128 corporate legal department professionals and GCs at US corporations, including people responsible for legal operations. The infographic separately describes Legal Tracker spend analytics sourced from more than 1,500 corporate law departments. The supplied material does not explain how these evidence bases are combined.
qs: The findings in the report are based on a survey that was conducted in July of 128 corporate legal department professionals and GCs, including those responsible for legal operations, at corporations across the United States.
Data in this year’s LDO Index Survey is comprised of real-world legal spend analytics gathered from Thomson Reuters’ Legal Tracker and sourced from more than 1,500 corporate law departments.

kp.k: Resource pressures motivate automation and anticipated insourcing
kp.d: The infographic reports that 56% of legal department professionals consider their departments under-resourced, 81% report increasing matter volumes, and 55% report flat or decreasing departmental budgets. Against these pressures, 46% expect more work to move in-house and 73% plan to use advanced technology to automate legal tasks and reduce costs. These plans and expectations are not demonstrated automation savings or completed insourcing.
qs: More than half of legal department professionals surveyed report that they see their department as *under-resourced*
Almost three-quarters of respondents say they plan to use advanced technology to automate legal tasks and reduce costs
report increasing matter volumes.
expect to bring more work in-house.

kp.k: Technology investment persists despite constrained departmental budgets
kp.d: Article 1 reports that 59% of respondents are increasing technology use and 88% have stable or increasing technology budgets. The infographic reports that 51% have flat or unchanged legal technology budgets. These figures distinguish technology spending from overall departmental budget constraints and do not establish effective usage or financial returns.
qs: 59% of respondents say they are increasing their use of technology tools, and an overwhelming 88% say they have stable or increasing tech budgets to make that happen.
report flat or no change in
legal tech budgets.

kp.k: Rapid deployment ambitions coexist with slow technological change
kp.d: Article 1 reports that departments seeking fast, large-scale technology deployments increased from 3% last year to 12%, a four-fold rise, and predicts further growth as AI adoption intensifies. Nevertheless, 45% characterize their department's pace of technology advancement as slow. The prediction of continued acceleration is the article's interpretation, not an observed future outcome.
qs: As a result, the number of legal departments that are looking to implement fast, large-scale technology deployments is surging.
Although it’s currently only 12%, that’s a four-fold increase from just 3% last year, and it’s likely to continue climbing as the race to adopt AI tools intensifies.
yet almost half also characterize the pace of technology advancement in their departments as *slow*.

kp.k: Existing technology underutilization signals weak AI readiness
kp.d: Article 1 argues that adoption does not establish effectiveness: established tools such as legal research, spend management and e-discovery remain underutilized despite being considered valuable when used. It identifies inadequate training, lack of awareness and integration failures as reasons, treating these operational weaknesses as warnings for AI implementation rather than evidence that AI cannot deliver benefits.
qs: Yet, adoption does not necessarily mean effectiveness
The reasons for underutilization are many-fold, including inadequate training, lack of awareness, and failure to properly integrate technology solutions.
The underutilization of existing technology in legal departments isn't just a current operational challenge — it's a warning signal about departments’ readiness for the AI era.

kp.k: Contract AI and GenAI already face utilization problems
kp.d: Article 1 reports that contract AI tools are more than twice as likely to be considered underutilized as effectively used, while GenAI tools struggle to reach an even split between those categories. It also says departments are more likely to report not yet adopting GenAI but seeking procurement over the next 24 months, presenting this early adoption stage as an opportunity to prepare.
qs: Contract AI tools are currently more than twice as likely to be considered underutilized than being used effectively.
Generative AI (GenAI) tools also are struggling to achieve an even split between underutilization and effective usage.
Legal departments are more likely to report that they have not yet adopted GenAI tools but are looking to procure them over the next 24 months, so there is still time to prepare.

kp.k: AI implementation requires workflow, role and governance changes
kp.d: Article 1 recommends auditing existing technology utilization, prioritizing tools against pressing departmental needs, ensuring sufficient implementation capacity, and providing training reinforced through use cases and best practices. It argues that AI will require new processes, policies and governance, plus more substantial changes to workflows, role definitions and work practices than previous deployments. Operational transformation is presented as conditional on planning and change management.
qs: Assess the current utilization of existing legal tech solutions and use this assessment to prioritize investment towards those tools that address the department’s most pressing needs.
Deploying new technologies requires resources, and department leaders need to make sure there is sufficient implementation bandwidth.
Unlike other technologies, AI is likely to require new processes, policies, and governance frameworks in order to be most impactful.
In addition, AI adoption will require more substantial changes to departmental workflows, role definitions, and work practices than previous technology deployments.
And by sharing use cases and best practices, leaders can reinforce training and continually drive awareness.

kp.k: Legal operations expands beyond cost control toward organizational value
kp.d: The report announcement describes legal operations as moving beyond its original cost-control emphasis toward systems, processes and technology. It says GCs increasingly enlist operations teams to improve departmental efficiency and effectiveness and articulate legal's value to corporate management. This is a reported evolution in the buyer-side operations function, not a claim about law-firm staffing structures.
qs: Moving beyond its origins as primarily a cost-control function, legal operations efforts are expanding to focus more strongly on systems, processes, and technology.
corporate general counsel (GCs) are facing additional pressure to show the value that their in-house legal departments can offer the organization.
LDO teams are increasingly being enlisted to join their GCs in this pursuit of value and its articulation to management.

kp.k: Dedicated operations staff does not ensure specialist leadership
kp.d: The infographic reports that 82% of respondents have at least one dedicated legal operations role, while 45% of those responsible for leading operations identify as a GC tasked with running legal operations. It explicitly distinguishes having dedicated staff from having senior-level operations leadership.

kp.k: Operations specialists correlate with different purchasing and management practices
kp.d: Respondents associate specialist legal operations leadership with increased technology use, growing technology budgets, more sophisticated spend management, and more frequent use of ALSPs and alternative fee arrangements than GC-led operations. The announcement contrasts specialists' efficiency and cost-control focus with GCs' client-service and legal-quality priorities, suggesting potential complementarity. It repeatedly cautions that department size, resources and maturity may explain disparities, rather than establishing a causal leadership effect.
qs: legal departments with legal ops professionals overseeing operations saw an increased use of legal technology tools, along with a growing budget for these solutions — as well as a more sophisticated management of the department’s legal spend, according to respondents.
Those with legal ops backgrounds also more commonly use alternative legal service providers and alternative fee arrangements, compared to GCs tasked with legal ops.
Legal ops backgrounders push for efficiency and stronger cost-control, while GCs tend to prioritize client service and the quality of legal work.
it is important to remember that these disparities may be influenced by differences in department size, resources, and maturity.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Thomson Reuters Institute presents AI as a potential means of improving in-house efficiency and reducing costs, but says adoption alone does not ensure effective use or operational transformation.
pts.d: Article 1 claims that AI-powered tools are among the fastest-growing solutions adopted by legal departments, while warning that they are reproducing existing technology-underutilization patterns. Contract AI tools are reported to be more than twice as likely to be considered underutilized as effectively used; GenAI tools are described as struggling to achieve an even split. TRI predicts that AI implementation will require new governance, processes, and more substantial changes to workflows, roles, and work practices than earlier technology deployments. It also predicts continued growth in appetite for fast, large-scale technology deployments as the AI adoption race intensifies. The infographic reports that 70% expect GenAI to influence interactions with internal business stakeholders, without specifying the nature of that influence. Zach Warren's Article 2 and the infographic report plans to automate legal tasks and reduce costs, but these refer to advanced technology generally, not exclusively AI. These are reported intentions and expectations, rather than demonstrated AI productivity or cost-saving outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims draw primarily on the 2025 LDO Index's survey of corporate legal professionals; the supplied material reports perceptions and plans rather than measured AI performance.
pts.d: Warren identifies the survey as involving 128 US corporate legal department professionals and GCs, including those responsible for legal operations, conducted in July in the context of the 2025 report. Article 1 attributes technology-underutilization findings to the Index, but supplies no detailed denominator or methodology for the Contract AI and GenAI comparisons. It reports that 59% are increasing technology-tool use, 88% have stable or increasing technology budgets, and 12% seek fast, large-scale deployments, compared with 3% last year. The infographic reports that 73% plan technology-based automation to reduce costs, 45% characterize technology advancement as slow, and 70% expect GenAI to influence internal stakeholder interactions. These general technology figures should not be treated as AI-specific adoption rates. The infographic additionally states that the Index contains Legal Tracker spend analytics sourced from more than 1,500 corporate law departments; the supplied text does not connect those analytics to a measured AI effect or explain their relationship to the 128-person survey. The operational-transformation prediction and implementation recommendations are TRI's interpretation and advice, not results of a reported controlled test.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source describes early-stage adoption in 2025 and procurement intentions over the next 24 months; projected benefits depend on organizational preparation rather than immediate gains from purchasing tools.
pts.d: Article 1 says departments are more likely to report not yet having adopted GenAI but looking to procure it over the next 24 months. Its prediction that large-scale deployment appetite will continue rising has no fixed endpoint. Successful AI use is conditioned on technology audits, prioritizing departmental needs, sufficient implementation capacity, appropriate policies and governance, workflow changes, training, and continuing awareness through use cases and best practices. Inadequate training, lack of awareness, and poor integration are identified as reasons existing tools are underutilized. The source does not quantify when savings or transformation will materialize. Warren also qualifies observed differences between departments led operationally by legal ops professionals and those led by GCs: department size, resources, and maturity may explain the differences, so the article does not establish that leadership background causes greater technology effectiveness.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected population is primarily the corporate buyer side: in-house lawyers, legal operations teams, GCs, and their internal business stakeholders.
pts.d: The survey concerns US corporate legal departments. The infographic reports that 56% consider their departments under-resourced, 81% report increasing matter volumes, and 46% expect more work to be brought in-house. Against this background, AI and broader automation are presented as ways to support departmental efficiency and cost control, not as demonstrated causes of insourcing. Lawyers and staff would need training and changes to work practices; departmental leaders would need to provide implementation capacity and governance. GCs and legal operations professionals are responsible for demonstrating value to corporate management, while internal business stakeholders are expected to experience changes in interactions with legal departments through GenAI. Warren reports that departments overseen by legal ops professionals use more technology and more commonly use ALSPs and alternative fee arrangements than those where GCs run operations; these are contextual associations, not claimed AI-driven changes in provider markets. The supplied material does not predict lawyer job losses, law-firm staffing changes, or public access-to-justice effects.
